t.6.74.1: Having thus spoken to Saumitri, Vibhīṣaṇa, filled with joy, took him, bow in hand, and went off in haste.
t.6.74.2: Then, having gone a short distance and entered a great forest, Vibhīṣaṇa showed Lakṣmaṇa that deed.
t.6.74.3: The radiant brother of Rāvaṇa pointed out to Lakṣmaṇa the banyan tree, dreadful to behold, resembling a dark rain-cloud.
t.6.74.4: Here the mighty son of Rāvaṇa, having first made an offering to the spirits, then afterwards proceeds to battle.
t.6.74.5: Then the rākṣasa becomes invisible to all beings; he slays his enemies in battle and binds them with his excellent arrows.
t.6.74.6: Before he reaches the banyan tree, destroy that mighty son of Rāvaṇa with sharp arrows, together with his chariot, his horses and his charioteer.
t.6.74.7: Saying "So be it," the greatly radiant Saumitri, the delight of his friends, stood firm there, drawing his splendid bow.
t.6.74.8: That mighty son of Rāvaṇa, Indrajit, clad in armour, bearing a sword and with his banner raised, was seen in his chariot that shone with the colour of fire.
t.6.74.9: The one of great splendour said to the unconquered Paulastya: "I challenge you in battle; give me a proper fight."
t.6.74.10: Thus addressed, the greatly radiant and high-spirited son of Rāvaṇa, seeing Vibhīṣaṇa there, spoke harsh words.
t.6.74.11: Here you were born and here you grew up; you are my father's own brother. How can you, my paternal uncle, betray his son, O Rākṣasa?
t.6.74.13: You are to be pitied, O evil-minded one, and to be condemned by the virtuous, you who, abandoning your own kinsmen, have come to the servitude of others.
t.6.74.12: O evil-minded one, for you neither kinship, nor friendship, nor lineage carries any weight, nor brotherhood born of the same womb, nor dharma, O defiler of dharma!
t.6.74.14: With your feeble understanding you do not grasp this great difference: how far apart are living among one's own kin and taking refuge with base strangers!
t.6.74.15: Whether a stranger be virtuous, or one's own kinsman be devoid of virtue, the kinsman without virtue is still the better; he who is a stranger remains a stranger.
t.6.74.16: And such is this pitilessness of yours, O night-roamer, that harshness is possible for you, our own kinsman, O younger brother of Rāvaṇa.
t.6.74.17: Thus addressed by his brother's son, Vibhīṣaṇa replied: "Why do you boast, O Rākṣasa, as though you did not know my character?"
t.6.74.18: O son of the lord of the rākṣasas, O wicked one, give up your harshness out of the respect you owe me. Although I was born in the family of rākṣasas whose deeds are cruel, my character is not that of a rākṣasa, for this is the foremost virtue of men.
t.6.74.20: The seizing of others' property, the violation of others' wives, and excessive distrust of friends: these three faults bring about ruin.
t.6.74.19: I take no delight in cruelty, nor indeed do I delight in unrighteousness; how then is a brother cast out by a brother of contrary character?
t.6.74.21: The dreadful slaughter of the great sages, strife with all the gods, arrogance and wrath, enmity and hostility.
t.6.74.22: These faults of my brother, destroyers of his life and sovereignty, concealed his virtues as clouds conceal the mountains.
t.6.74.23: Because of these faults I abandoned my brother, your father. This city of Laṅkā is no more, nor are you, nor is your father.
t.6.74.24: Arrogant, childish and ill-mannered are you, O rākṣasa; bound as you are by the noose of Time, say to me whatever you wish.
t.6.74.26: Having assailed the two Kākutsthas, you cannot go on living. Fight in battle with Lakṣmaṇa, lord among men; slain, you will accomplish the work of the gods in the abode of Yama.
t.6.74.25: Today ruin has come upon you; what will you say here now? You cannot enter the banyan tree, O vilest of rākṣasas!
t.6.74.27: Display your own strength, raised up and ready; make full expenditure of all your weapons and arrows. For having come within range of Lakṣmaṇa's arrows, you will not today go away alive with your army.
